masthead_title: The dollar's climb is this morning's biggest signal — and it's chip stocks, not the broad market, absorbing the pressure.
regime_line: The dollar just logged its strongest five-day run of this cycle — DXY up 1.1% to 103.41, this run's largest flag at z +2.44, a move big enough to count as tightening on its own, while the 10-year Treasury's own climb put it back above a level last traded in July 2007 (today's lead History-check fact, below). Friday's reversal in chip stocks (AMD −8.75%, Dell −7.18%, Cisco −6.24%) pulled the Nasdaq down, even though the S&P 500 and the average stock barely moved.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — five resolved over the weekend's backlog, one confirmed

Two runs failed closed on data gaps (11-12, 11-13), so five open claims came due without a reconciliation in between. All five are checked against Friday's close before any new narrative below.

  • CL-0067 (hawkish repricing holding through mid-November, due 2026-11-17) — confirmed early. The 2-year Treasury closed at or above the test's 4.73% bar on all three sessions with data in the window (Nov. 10: 4.73%, Nov. 12: 4.86%, Nov. 13: 4.88% — Nov. 11 is a data gap), already clearing the "3 of 5 sessions" bar with one session still to come, and it never closed near the 4.51% refute line. The repricing held.
  • CL-0064 (stock/credit divergence, due today) — expired, mixed. The S&P 500 never got close to the credit-read trigger (window low $7,520.93 on Nov. 10; closed Friday at $7,561.67, well above the $7,353.73 line), and HY OAS cleared its own flag (z +1.38). But IG OAS is still flagged (z +1.70), so the equity-read confirm condition — both credit series clear, S&P above $7,376.86 — wasn't fully met either. Equities were closer to right than credit was, but neither side won outright.
  • CL-0066 (credit stabilizing vs. just pausing, due Friday) — expired, inconclusive. HY OAS cleared the flag line (z +1.38) but IG OAS didn't (z +1.70) — one leg of credit eased, the other didn't, so neither the full-stabilization nor the renewed-divergence test fired.
  • CL-0060 (Vistra's post-election selloff as durable repricing, due 11-12) — expired, unresolved — leaning refuted. Vistra never stayed flat-to-lower from its $120.29 base (it closed $134.51 on 11-12, +11.8%) and never technically crossed the $135 refute line either — it got within 49 cents before easing to $133.01 Friday. The letter of the test says unresolved; the direction says overreaction, mostly recovered.
  • CL-0061 (FIS's guidance-cut selloff as durable skepticism, due 11-12) — expired, unresolved. FIS broke its own "every session at or below $29.76" confirm path once (closed $30.21 on 11-11) but never approached the $34 refute line (window high $30.21, closed $28.36 on 11-12). Neither durable skepticism nor a clean overreaction.
story_html:
Friday's coverage (CNBC, Benzinga) led with a reversal in chip stocks: AMD fell 8.75% to $534.06, Dell 7.18% to $344.53, and Cisco 6.24% to $95.64, even though Cisco had beaten its first-quarter estimates and raised full-year guidance that same week — reporting attributed the drop to profit-taking and margin concerns rather than any demand-side news. Benzinga's wrap tied the move to the broader chip complex giving back the week's sharp rally; the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell roughly 3.4% and Nvidia extended a losing streak heading into its own earnings Tuesday after the close. No distinct, dated catalyst for Dell specifically surfaced in today's search — worth saying plainly rather than guessing at one.

This system's own pull backs the headline move but complicates the "AI trade in doubt" framing those headlines imply. All three names gave back more than just Friday: this system's own closes show Dell and Cisco each ended the week lower than where they started it (Dell $344.53 vs. Monday's $346.31; Cisco $95.64 vs. Monday's $98.65), while AMD still closed the week up 5.0% from Monday despite Friday's drop — a partial round-trip, not a one-day shock, after all three rallied hard Monday through Thursday. And the damage stayed narrow: the S&P 500 fell just 0.36% and the equal-weight average (RSP) actually rose 0.20% (Unit 6's breadth tool), while Technology (XLK) underperformed the index by 1.65 percentage points and Consumer Staples (XLP) outperformed by 1.78 — money rotating out of chips and into defensives, not a broad selloff. Credit didn't confirm stress either: HY OAS eased below its flag line (z +1.38) even as IG OAS stayed flagged (z +1.70), a mixed, not alarming, credit read.

The move this system's own data flags loudest, though, sat outside Friday's headlines entirely: the dollar. DXY has climbed every session this week, now at its highest level in six months (chart of the day, below) — and copper, priced in dollars worldwide, fell to this run's second-largest flag (z −2.07) over the same stretch. That's the dollar-transmission channel Unit 5 covered, showing up live. Today's calendar carries a scheduled, high-impact speech from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at noon ET — a known event, not a surprise, so this morning frames what to watch rather than guessing the outcome (new claim CL-0068, Flags, below).
dashboard_interp_html:
Every Treasury tenor rose this week, but the move was front-end-led. The 3-month bill is flat on the day but up 15bp over five sessions to 4.32% (z +1.85, flagged; 53rd percentile since 1977 but the 72nd of the last 30 years — an 18-point gap, not quite the 20-point bar that forces dual citation, but close). The 2-year — the part of the curve that runs as a live poll of Fed expectations — rose 2bp to 4.88% and 42bp over five sessions (z +1.77, flagged; 54th percentile since 1976 but the 84th of the last 30 years, † a 30-point gap). The 10-year rose 5bp to 5.15% (z +1.45, just under the flag line; 48th/86th, † — today's lead History-check fact, below, where that same gap is the whole story) and the 30-year rose 4bp to 5.47% (z +1.26; 48th/84th, †). Why this matters: a front-end-led rise like this is mostly a repricing of how many more times the Fed moves, not a growth or inflation story for the next decade — closer to what sets a new CD rate than a 30-year mortgage quote, though five straight sessions of this did eventually touch the long end too.

The curve's two slices disagreed on direction this week: 2s10s flattened 11bp to 27bp (29th/31st percentile, no real gap, nowhere near inversion) while 3m10y widened 16bp to 83bp (31st/38th) — the long end and the very front moved more than the belly did, a lopsided version of this week's front-end-led story.

The 10-year TIPS real yield — what Treasuries pay after inflation, dated Thursday — rose 8bp to 2.86% (z +1.65, flagged), while the 10-year breakeven — the market's own inflation forecast baked into nominal yields — rose 4bp to 2.24% (z −1.14, not flagged). Nearly all of this week's 10-year move was a real-rate story, not an inflation story (Unit 2). Why this matters: a real-rate-led rise raises the actual cost of borrowing after accounting for inflation — the kind of move that eventually shows up in variable-rate loans and new mortgage quotes, not just Fed-futures pricing.

Credit split in opposite directions this week, which is the one piece of good news in an otherwise tightening tape. HY OAS (dated Thursday, the usual one-day lag) eased 10bp to 3.20% (z +1.38, cleared its own flag line; 70th percentile of its own ~3-year record, §4F, marked *). IG OAS (also Thursday) eased just 1bp to 0.89% (z +1.70, still flagged; 61st percentile of its own ~3-year record, also *). Why this matters: lenders to junk-rated borrowers got slightly less worried this week even as lenders to investment-grade borrowers stayed about as cautious as they were — two different risk gauges, not one, and they're not telling quite the same story right now (Unit 3).

The dollar is this week's loudest single move. DXY rose 24bp Friday and 111bp (1.1%) over five sessions to 103.41 — this run's largest flag (z +2.44; 83rd percentile of the last 30 years, 74th since 1971, no real gap between the two). SOFR (dated Thursday) ticked up 1bp to 3.90% (z +1.45, not flagged; 45th percentile since 1954 but the 67th of the last 30 years, †, a 22-point gap). Fed balance-sheet and TGA readings are last Wednesday's H.4.1/DTS release, still carried forward — both structurally modern-only instruments with no pre-2008 "normal" to compare against (§4F). ON RRP ticked up to $0.33B (z −0.48, not flagged; also modern-only). Why this matters: a dollar this strong raises the local-currency cost of dollar debt for borrowers outside the U.S. and makes dollar-priced commodities more expensive everywhere else — exactly the transmission loop behind this morning's copper and gold weakness (Story, above; Cross-asset, below).
history_html:
Today's deepest echo is the 10-year Treasury, now 5.15% after first reaching this level Sep. 24 — held on 16 of 35 sessions since. Before this run, last traded this high in July 2007; this run's own high, 5.31% on Oct. 5, last matched May 2002. The two lenses disagree: the 86th percentile of the last 30 years, but just the 48th percentile of the full 64-year record — unusual lately, unremarkable across the full sweep, since that record folds in the double-digit yields of the late 1970s-80s.

The then-vs-now panel pairs today against July 2007 (below). The 10-year lines up almost exactly (5.15% now vs. 5.16% then) and the curve shape is close too. What's different: back then the Fed was headed toward cutting; this run's own front-end-led climb (Dashboard, above) points the other way.

Second fact: the 10-year TIPS real yield sits at the 99.5th percentile of its own 23-year record (TIPS only exist since 2003). The Cleveland Fed's longer model, back to 1982, reads milder: 80th percentile of the last 30 years, just the 54th since 1982 — same concept, two different numbers.

Third: the 2-year's 141bp rise this year is the 7th-largest through this date in 50 years — bigger only in 2022, 1994, 1978. In the 8 similar surges since 1977, the S&P 500 was lower a year later in 3 of 8 (any 12-month stretch since 1962: 24.4%), and a recession began within two years in 2 of 8 (any two-year stretch since 1962: 27.4%). Client-ready line: today's level has been seen before, just rarely, with a very different Fed; the speed this year — top-10 of 50 — is what's genuinely unusual.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically, plus the top-50 megacaps; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) or a sector ETF diverging ≥1.5pp from SPX, never by seeming interesting. 28 name candidates and 2 sector divergences qualified Friday; the cap holds at 3 names + 1 sector note.

AMD −8.75% (534.06, from 585.30) — what happened: the day's largest S&P 500 decliner, and the clearest single name behind today's chart of the day. Stated reason: part of a broad reversal in the chip/AI-hardware complex that gave back the week's sharp rally, with no distinct AMD-specific news found (Benzinga, CNBC Friday coverage); the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 3.4% the same session. Read-through: mostly idiosyncratic to the group's own week-long rally unwinding, layered on persistent AI-capex-cycle doubt (Tier 3, below) — not a fresh demand signal either way.

Cisco −6.24% (95.64, from 102.01) — what happened: fell despite beating its fiscal first-quarter estimates and raising full-year guidance days earlier. Stated reason: reporting (CNBC's Friday markets coverage) attributed the drop to profit-taking and margin concerns rather than any new demand-side news — a sell-the-beat reaction inside the broader chip-sector reversal. Read-through: idiosyncratic to positioning around an already-digested earnings beat, not a new signal about enterprise networking demand.

Dell −7.18% (344.53, from 371.17) — what happened: the day's third-largest S&P 500 decliner, swept into the same hardware/chip reversal. Stated reason: no distinct, credibly dated company-specific catalyst surfaced in today's search — stated plainly rather than inferred, per §5. Read-through: idiosyncratic to the group's reversal; nothing today's search could confirm about Dell's own AI-server business specifically.

Sector note: Technology (XLK) underperformed the S&P 500 by 1.65 percentage points (−2.01% vs. −0.36%) while Consumer Staples (XLP) outperformed by 1.78pp (+1.42%) — the mirror image of the same move: money rotating out of chips/tech and into defensives, not a broad market selloff (Unit 6's breadth tool, confirmed again by RSP's own +0.20% day).
chart_of_day_why: DXY carries this run's largest |z| flag (+2.44), the clearest single mover behind today's tightening read — up 1.1% over five straight sessions to a fresh high for this run, even as chip stocks cracked and the broader index barely budged. It's also the series behind this morning's copper and gold weakness (Story, above), the dollar-transmission channel Unit 5 built.
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH underperformed SPY by about 2.6 percentage points Friday (−2.99% vs. −0.36%), this run's largest single-series flag (z −2.23) and the sharpest one-day underperformance in several weeks — even though SMH is still up 4.9% over the last five sessions. The reversal reads as giving back the week's sharp rally (Movers, above) rather than a fresh demand signal; Nvidia reports Tuesday after the close, the next real test of the cycle's demand side.

Weekly issuance/spread note: no fresh, dated hyperscaler-issuance or vendor-financing news surfaced in today's search. HY/IG OAS (dated Thursday, Dashboard above) split for the first time in weeks — HY easing below its flag, IG staying flagged — the live reading on financing-side risk appetite heading into Nvidia's print. calendar_note_html:
Today: a light data calendar but one high-impact item — Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak at noon ET, plus routine remarks from Governors Williams, Barr, and Hammack through the day. The Empire State Manufacturing Index (8:30am ET) is a low-impact regional read, forecast 17.6 vs. 25.5 prior. Tuesday brings Nvidia's earnings after the close and Wednesday brings Retail Sales, a high-impact release this week.

Why this matters to the current regime: today's calendar is a known, scheduled event, not a surprise — so this morning frames what to watch rather than guessing the outcome (§4E). A hawkish-sounding Warsh would fit neatly with this week's dollar and front-end-rate climb (Dashboard, above); a dovish-sounding one would be the first real test of whether that climb has further to run. New claim CL-0068 (Flags, below) is built to grade it tomorrow.
concept_title: A fourth vote joins the hierarchy — the dollar tends to side with rates, not credit, because both price off the same real-rate input
concept_html:
Segment 5 showed the hierarchy splitting three ways — rates, credit, and breadth each answering a different question. This week adds a fourth voice: the dollar. DXY's climb to this run's largest flag (z +2.44, Chart of the day, above) isn't really a separate opinion from the front-end-led rate rise (Dashboard, above) — both are priced off the same thing, how much the Fed is expected to keep rates elevated, which is why they tend to move together rather than disagree. That's different from credit's job: credit prices default and liquidity risk, a genuinely separate question from the rate path, which is exactly why HY OAS eased this week (z +1.38, cleared its flag) even as rates and the dollar both climbed — not a contradiction, just two different gauges answering two different questions, with the dollar siding with rates rather than with credit because of what it's actually built to measure.

The practical test: when the dollar and rates move together, that's not independent confirmation the way credit agreeing with equities would be — it's closer to the same signal measured twice. Independent confirmation has to come from a gauge pricing a genuinely different risk, which is why credit (and, this week, breadth — RSP's +0.20% day even as the S&P fell) still carry more weight in the hierarchy than a second rates-linked series would.
client_translation: The dollar getting stronger and interest rates rising together this week aren't two separate warning signs — they're basically the same signal (the market expecting the Fed to stay higher for longer) showing up in two places, which is different from credit markets actually getting nervous about defaults, and they haven't.
client_lens_html:
“Why did [AMD/Dell/Cisco] fall so much Friday?” Mostly the chip sector giving back a sharp rally from earlier in the week, not fresh bad news — Cisco actually beat estimates and raised guidance days before it fell. Worth separating "the stock gave back a big run-up" from "something changed about the business," especially for clients who only see the headline percentage.

“Is the strong dollar going to hurt my international funds?” A stronger dollar does act as a drag on dollar-based returns from overseas holdings and on commodity prices generally (this morning's copper and gold weakness, Story above) — worth flagging if a client holds unhedged international exposure, though this week's move, while this run's largest, sits in the middle of the dollar's own 55-year range (History, above), not in record territory.

“The market seems fine, so why does my tech-heavy account feel rough?” The headline S&P 500 number (down just 0.36% Friday) hid a real split: the average stock was actually up on the day, while chip and hardware names got hit hard. An account concentrated in that corner of the market had a materially worse week than the index suggests.
